text.p: Europe's stock markets emerged bruised but not broken as the dust settled on Friday after Wall Street's mauling, and analysts said they should escape the worst of the damage even if the Dow continues to suffer.

Interest rate worries provoked a pounding for Wall Street on Thursday, with the Dow knocked 160 points or 2.3 percent lower, and nervous European bourses scuttled lower in sympathy as they opened on Friday.

In London, Europe's biggest stock market, the FTSE 100 index of blue-chip shares opened one percent weaker, while in Paris the CAC-40 index dived 1.61 percent. Germany's DAX-30 started 0.33 percent lower after a 1.92 percent drop on Thursday.

But all three markets picked themselves off the floor as the morning progressed. Analysts said their stoic performance showed European markets had decoupled enough from the U.S. to withstand a further Wall Street hammering without too much pain.
But they warned that Europe could not expect to escape completely unscathed if the Dow came under attack again.

"A serious correction on Wall Street would have a significant impact on Europe, at least in the near term," said David Aserkoff, strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston. "The fact is that global security markets are just that -- global."
But after the initial blow, Europe had the scope to bounce back faster than the U.S. market, Aserkoff said.

"The fundamentals in the U.S. are very different from the fundamentals in Europe. The business cycles in the two regions are vastly different," he said. "We would see Europe being able to significantly outperform the U.S."
Wall Street's battering was caused by the growing conviction that U.S. interest rates will be raised on March 25 for the first time in two years.
But supporters of the decoupling argument point out that the situation in Europe is completely different.

Economies there are still struggling to emerge from recession so the interest-rate outlook is bullish for equities. And corporate earnings in Europe are expected to be on an upward track in coming months, supporting equity markets
Meanwhile, bond yields have been falling in Europe but have been steady to higher in the U.S., making Wall Street much more vulnerable to switching into bonds than Europe, analysts say.

But the decoupling argument also hangs crucially on the strength of the dollar. If it retreats from its current strong levels, Wall Street stocks will cheapen relative to European equities and any benefits of decoupling will be blunted.

"The key to decoupling is the currency," said Mike Young, director of European investment strategy at Goldman Sachs. "Any tendency for the dollar to go down, and a falling U.S. market would create an irresistible pull on European equities."
If the dollar stays firm, buoyed by expectations of further U.S. rate rises, then European markets will weather a Wall Street tumble relatively well, he said.
"While European equities might go down on the day, there would probably be a tendency to recover on the back of continued strong upgrades to earnings expectations," Young told Reuters.

Another risk to decoupling would be a sharp rise in U.S. bond yields which pulled European yields higher and took the ratio of equity to bond yields to a level which made equities vulnerable. But Young said this was unlikely.
"There is very little risk of an increase in short term interest rates in Europe, " he said.

"The real risk in the present environment is that the pull of higher U.S. yields at the long end would cause European yields to rise as well. But we think the long end in the U.S. has already discounted an interest rate rise, so European markets will see just a modest tendency for rates to rise."
Britain's situation is different from the rest of Europe -- its interest rates are already on an upward trajectory and its business cycle is closer to the U.S. than Germany.
But bond yields have followed the European pattern, leaving yield ratios less stretched than the U.S., and fundamentals should allow the FTSE to outperform Wall Street, analysts said.

"The UK has got over the turn in the interest rate cycle, whereas U.S. rates have been on hold for some time and the market is getting nervous about the transition," said Corey Miller, strategist at Credit Lyonnais Laing.
"If the U.S. dives then in the short term you have to be a little concerned," he said.

"But fundamentally we are OK. Some of the corporate results we've had have been better than expected and people are reining back their interest rate expectations. The market is flush with cash. So there is a firm undertone."
